title: Med-SegLens: Latent-Level Model Diffing for Interpretable Medical Image Segmentation
claim: A staged procedure turns model activations into sparse interpretable latents, then compares them across datasets to diagnose shift and enable intervention.
layout: 4 labeled panels A–D, left-to-right, SAE schematic with trapezoid encoder/decoder
description: A wide four-stage strip with the stages labeled A to D across the top and separated by dashed vertical lines. A shows brain MRI slices (SSA glioma, adult glioma, healthy, pediatric glioma) feeding into a stacked segmentation model with Layer 1 to Layer N, where Layer M is highlighted with a bold outline. B shows the activation vector as blue squares passing through a trapezoid encoder, a latent column, an activation function box, a sparse latent h(z), a trapezoid decoder, and a reconstructed activation vector. C shows a faded latent column and an active one, with arrows pointing to labels such as 'Activates on Edema' and 'Activates on White Matter'. D shows SSA and PED glioma latent columns with crossing lines, mapping to PED-specific, SSA-specific and shared latent blocks. The palette is mostly blue, and the eye goes first to the MRI images and the highlighted Layer M.
caption: Overview of the proposed framework. We extract intermediate activations from a medical image segmentation model (A) and train sparse autoencoders on these activations to learn interpretable latent features (B). Using our Auto-Interp method, we assign semantic meaning to the learned latents (C). Finally, we perform cross-dataset model diffing to characterize domain shift and enable targeted latent-level interventions (D).
abstract: Modern segmentation models achieve strong predictive performance but remain largely opaque, limiting our ability to diagnose failures, understand dataset shift, or intervene in a principled manner. We introduce \textbf{Med-SegLens}, a model-diffing framework that decomposes segmentation model activations into interpretable latent features using sparse autoencoders trained on SegFormer and U-Net. Through cross-architecture and cross-dataset latent alignment across healthy, adult, pediatric, and sub-Saharan African glioma cohorts, we identify a stable backbone of shared representations, while dataset shift is driven by differential reliance on population-specific latents. We show that these latents act as causal bottlenecks for segmentation failures, and that targeted latent-level interventions can correct errors and improve cross-dataset adaption without retraining, recovering performance in 70% of failure cases and improving Dice score from 39.4% to 74.2%. Our results demonstrate that latent-level model diffing provides a practical and mechanistic tool for diagnosing failures and mitigating dataset shift in segmentation models.
